title: Guns, Germs, and Steel
author: Jared Diamond

parts.title: Yali's question
text: In July 1972, on a beach in New Guinea, Jared Diamond was asked a question he spent twenty-five years trying to answer. He was there to study birds. The man asking was Yali, a local politician, who wanted to know why white people had developed so much cargo, meaning steel axes, matches, medicines and all the goods of the modern world, while New Guineans had so little of their own.

Put more broadly: why did Europeans and Asians conquer the Americas, Australia and much of Africa, rather than the other way round? Guns, Germs, and Steel is Diamond's answer, a history of the last 13,000 years, since the end of the last Ice Age, when people on every continent were still hunters and gatherers.

Diamond rejects the racist answer, that some peoples are smarter than others, and he does so from long experience. After years of working with New Guineans, he says they struck him as, on average, more alert and curious than the Europeans and Americans he knew. His own answer is that history followed different courses for different peoples because their environments differed. The continents dealt very different hands, and the peoples who held the best cards were the ones whose descendants went on to conquer.

His method is to separate proximate causes from ultimate ones. The proximate causes of conquest are the things in the title: guns, germs and steel, along with ships, horses, writing and centralised states. The ultimate causes are why those things arose in some places much earlier than in others. Diamond, trained as a physiologist and later a professor of geography, treats history the way a scientist treats a field where experiments are impossible: he looks for natural experiments that history has already run.

parts.title: One afternoon at Cajamarca
text: Diamond's emblem of conquest is a single meeting. On 16 November 1532, at the town of Cajamarca in the highlands of Peru, the Spanish adventurer Francisco Pizarro, with 168 soldiers, met the Inca emperor Atahuallpa, who was surrounded by an army of about 80,000. The Spaniards seized the emperor and slaughtered thousands of his followers, without losing a man. They held Atahuallpa for a ransom of a room filled with gold, and then executed him.

How could so few defeat so many? Diamond lists the advantages. The Spaniards had steel swords and armour against stone and wooden clubs. They had horses, which no Inca soldier had ever faced. They had guns, though these mattered less than steel. Writing let them learn from earlier conquests, while Atahuallpa knew nothing of what Spaniards had done in Mexico. And they had already been helped by germs: smallpox, spreading south ahead of the Europeans, had killed the previous emperor and his heir, setting off the civil war that Atahuallpa had just won.

The same advantages appear again and again. On the Chatham Islands east of New Zealand, Diamond describes a smaller natural experiment. Two peoples descended from the same Polynesian ancestors had gone separate ways. The Moriori, on remote, cold islands where crops would not grow, became a few thousand hunter-gatherers with simple tools and a tradition of settling disputes peacefully. The Maori of New Zealand became dense farming societies with warriors and chiefs. In 1835, about 900 Maori arrived by ship, armed with guns and clubs, and killed or enslaved the Moriori.
So the question becomes why the advantages were all on the Spanish side. Diamond traces each of them back to one thing: food production.

parts.title: The luck of the plants
text: Farming produces far more calories per acre than hunting and gathering, so it supports far more people. It also produces surpluses that can be stored, and stored food can feed people who do not farm: kings, priests, soldiers, metalworkers, scribes. Dense, settled populations with specialists are what eventually build ships and armies. Every advantage at Cajamarca grew out of farming that had started thousands of years earlier.

Yet farming arose independently in only a handful of places, perhaps as few as five and at most nine. The earliest was the Fertile Crescent of south-west Asia, by about 8500 BC. Diamond argues the region was lucky in its wild plants. Of the world's 56 grass species with the largest seeds, 32 grew wild in the Mediterranean climate of western Eurasia, and the Fertile Crescent had several of the best. Its first farmers started with a package of eight founder crops, among them two kinds of wheat, barley, lentils, peas and flax, which together gave carbohydrate, protein, oil and fibre.

Many wild plants are bitter or poisonous, and Diamond explains how farmers changed them, mostly without meaning to. Wild almonds contain a bitter compound that turns into cyanide; a rare tree without it would have been noticed, and its nuts gathered and planted. Wild wheat drops its seeds to scatter them, so the plants whose seeds stayed on the stalk were the ones harvested and sown again.

Other regions were less lucky. New Guinea did develop farming on its own, very early, but its crops were mainly taro and bananas, low in protein, and its only large domestic animal, the pig, had come from Asia. Highland New Guineans were skilled farmers with too little to work with. The difference between peoples, in Diamond's account, began with which plants happened to grow wild where they lived.

parts.title: Animals that would not be tamed
text: Big domestic animals mattered as much as crops. They gave meat, milk, leather and wool. They pulled ploughs, which let fewer farmers feed more people, and they carried goods and soldiers. The horse transformed war for thousands of years, until the First World War.

Diamond counts the candidates. The world has 148 species of large wild plant-eating mammals, weighing a hundred pounds or more, and before the twentieth century only 14 were domesticated. Thirteen of the fourteen came from Eurasia: sheep, goats, cattle, pigs and horses, and less widespread ones such as camels and water buffalo. South America had only the llama and alpaca. Sub-Saharan Africa, with its famous herds, contributed none, and Australia none.

He explains this with what he calls the Anna Karenina principle, after Tolstoy's opening line about happy and unhappy families. Domesticable animals are all alike, and every undomesticable animal is undomesticable in its own way. To be tamed, a species has to pass many tests at once. It has to eat something people can supply, grow fast, breed in captivity, tolerate humans, stay calm when penned and live in herds with a hierarchy a human can take over. Failing any one is enough.

Zebras look like horses, but they have a vicious temper and a habit of biting a person and not letting go. Gazelles panic and batter themselves against fences. Cheetahs will not breed in captivity, which is why princes who hunted with them had to capture new ones from the wild. The failures lay with the animals, Diamond stresses, and say nothing about the skills of the people who lived alongside them. Europeans in Africa tried to tame zebras in the nineteenth century, and failed too.

parts.title: The shape of the continents
text: Once crops and animals were domesticated somewhere, they could spread. How easily they spread depended on the shape of the land. Eurasia's main axis runs east to west. The Americas and Africa run mainly north to south.

This matters because places at the same latitude share the same length of day and similar seasons and diseases. A crop adapted to the Fertile Crescent could move west into Europe and east toward India with little change. Fertile Crescent crops reached Egypt and the Indus Valley within a few thousand years. Inventions such as the wheel and writing travelled the same roads.

In the Americas, crops had to cross deserts and a narrow, forested isthmus, and adapt to very different day lengths along the way. Corn took thousands of years to spread from Mexico to what is now the eastern United States. The llama never reached Mexico, so the Mesoamericans, who knew the principle of the wheel and put it on toys, never had an animal to pull a wheeled cart. The societies of Mexico and the Andes, Diamond notes, never met.

Africa shows the same pattern. Mediterranean crops could not cross the Sahara and the tropics to the southern tip of the continent, and cattle and horses were held back for long periods by diseases carried by tsetse flies. Australia, isolated and dry, had no domesticable plants or animals of any importance. Diamond's point is that the peoples of each continent inherited a geography as well as a set of wild species, and geography decided how far good ideas could travel.

parts.title: The lethal gift of livestock
text: The germs at Cajamarca had the same origin. The great killer diseases of history, measles, smallpox, tuberculosis and influenza, came from animals. They jumped to people who lived close to herds of cattle and pigs, and they survive only in large, dense populations, where there are always new people to infect. Farming societies built exactly those conditions.

Over thousands of years Eurasians paid a terrible price in epidemics and built up resistance. The peoples of the Americas, with few domestic animals and so few crowd diseases of their own, had none. When Europeans arrived, their diseases spread from tribe to tribe far ahead of the Europeans themselves. Diamond writes that throughout the Americas they killed an estimated 95 per cent of the population.

Smallpox reached Mexico in 1520 with an infected slave who came with a Spanish force from Cuba. The epidemic killed nearly half of the Aztecs, including their emperor, and helped Cortés take the capital. Over the following century, the population of Mexico fell from about twenty million to under two million. Diamond notes that the exchange was lopsided: the Americas gave Europe no lethal epidemic in return, with the possible exception of syphilis.
Neither the conquerors nor their victims understood any of this. Diamond reads the deaths as a consequence of who had lived with which animals for the previous ten thousand years.

parts.title: Writing, inventions and states
text: Writing, too, followed food production, because it was invented by and for complex societies with scribes to keep accounts. Diamond argues it was invented from scratch only a few times, certainly in Sumer before 3000 BC and in Mexico before 600 BC, possibly in Egypt and China. Everywhere else it was borrowed, as a finished system or as an idea. The Cherokee Sequoyah, around 1820, saw white settlers writing on paper and invented a whole set of written signs for his own language, without being able to read English.

Diamond also challenges the idea that necessity is the mother of invention. Often the invention comes first and finds its use later. When Thomas Edison built the phonograph in 1877, he listed its uses as recording the last words of the dying, reading books to the blind and teaching spelling. Playing music was low on his list, and when others later put phonographs into jukeboxes, Edison objected. What matters for a society is less who invents than whether it adopts and spreads inventions, and large, connected populations with many rival societies adopt more.

Societies can also turn their backs on technology. Japan took up guns from Portuguese traders in 1543 and became expert at making them, then largely gave them up over the following centuries, because the samurai class preferred the sword. Isolated as it was, Japan could afford to.

Finally, food production made possible the political machinery of conquest. Diamond traces the steps from small bands of hunters, through tribes and chiefdoms, to states with taxes and standing armies. He is unsentimental about these states, calling their rulers kleptocrats who take wealth from commoners and give some of it back in public services. But only centralised states could organise the voyages and armies that reached Cajamarca.

parts.title: Why Europe and not China
text: Diamond's last puzzle comes from within Eurasia. If geography favoured the whole continent, why did Europe rather than China, which for centuries led the world in technology, end up conquering the Americas? China had cast iron, the compass, gunpowder, paper and printing long before Europe.

His answer is unity. China's coastline is smooth, with no large islands or peninsulas, and its heartland is joined by two great river valleys, so it was unified early and stayed unified for long periods. That made a single decision binding on everyone. In the early fifteenth century China sent fleets of hundreds of ships across the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa. Then, after a power struggle at court, the voyages were stopped and the shipyards dismantled. One decision ended the age of Chinese exploration.

Europe's indented coastline and its mountain ranges kept it divided into many competing states. No single ruler could stop an idea everywhere. Christopher Columbus was turned down by one European prince after another before the king and queen of Spain agreed to pay for his voyage. Had Europe been one state, one refusal might have been the end of it.

He also asks why the Fertile Crescent, where so much began, lost its lead. Thousands of years of grazing and tree-felling turned a fragile environment into scrub and desert, and power moved west. Diamond ends by arguing that history can be studied as a science, as geology and evolutionary biology are, with natural experiments in place of laboratory ones. The answer to Yali's question, in Diamond's account, is that the gap between peoples has causes, and that none of them lies in the peoples themselves.
